title: A blessing for each food
hookLine: bread, grain, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit and everything else each have their own blessing

lines: SIX FOODS ON A KITCHEN TABLE.
A WAY OF LOOKING AT YOUR PLATE.
cards: A kitchen table: an apple, a strawberry, a slice of bread, a cookie, a glass of wine and a piece of cheese. Ask someone who keeps the blessings to bless them, and they won't say the same thing six times.
They'll say six different endings. The apple gets one; the strawberry gets another. The cookie and the bread differ too, though both are made from flour.
It sounds like a quiz. It's really a way of looking at what's on your plate. Today: hamotzi, and its cousins.

teach.b: After the six opening words, each food gets its own ending. Bread: hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz, who brings forth bread from the earth.
The words come from a psalm that says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, God makes things grow "to bring forth bread out of the earth."

Other grain foods, like cake, cookies or pasta: borei minei mezonot, who creates kinds of nourishment. Wine and grape juice: borei pri hagafen, who creates the fruit of the vine. Fruit from a tree: borei pri ha'etz.
Fruit and vegetables from the ground: borei pri ha'adamah, the fruit of the earth. Everything else, cheese, eggs, water, candy: shehakol nihyeh bidvaro, by whose word all things came to be.
So the apple gets tree, and the strawberry gets earth, because it grows on a low plant.

A banana, surprisingly, gets earth too: its plant isn't a tree in the rabbis' sense, since it doesn't keep its trunk year to year. Why bless food at all? The Talmud notices two verses that seem to disagree.
One psalm says: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Another says: "the earth hath He given to the children of men." Which is it?
The Talmud's answer: before the blessing, it's God's.

After the blessing, it's been given to you. Enjoying food without a blessing, the Talmud says, is like making personal use of something set aside for the Temple. The blessing is how the food changes hands.
And the endings make you look closely: did this grow on a tree, in the ground, from grain?

how: Before eating, observant Jews say the blessing that matches the food, bread, other grain foods, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit, or everything else, and the bread blessing covers the rest of a meal with bread.

o: a prayer for a good harvest in the fields
a song sung while kneading the dough for tomorrow's loaves
the blessing over bread, who brings it from the earth

games.q: which food gets which ending — tap the pairs.

s: a cookie gets the same blessing as bread
bread gets hamotzi; cookies and cake get mezonot.
a banana gets the blessing for fruit of the earth
the plant it grows on isn't a tree in the rabbis' sense.
the Talmud says before the blessing, food belongs to God
"the earth is the LORD's" before; "given to the children of men" after.

games.q: you're one of the rabbis. one psalm says the earth is the LORD's. another says the earth was given to people. how do you reconcile them?
o: before the blessing it's God's; after, it's given to you.
it belongs to whoever grew it.
games.why: the Talmud's answer: the blessing is the moment of asking. before it, the food is God's; after it, it's been given to you.

practice: Picture the next thing you'll eat and trace it back: a tree, like an apple or an orange; the ground, like a potato, a tomato, a strawberry; grain, like bread or pasta; or something else, like cheese or an egg.
Name its category, tree, earth, grain, bread, vine or everything else. If you pray, you can say its blessing when you eat it; if not, just pause and name where it came from.

wordCard.voice: Hamotzi. Who brings forth bread from the earth: the blessing over bread, one of six endings, each food with its own word.

orig.note: Hebrew: who brings forth. the full ending is hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz, who brings forth bread from the earth.
